name: Laz
confidence_why: Marr 1910 and Lacroix 2009 both put Laz stress on the penultimate syllable of nouns and other nominals, and both describe finite verbs as stressed instead on a negation, preverb or causative suffix, so the penultimate rule is secure while the record's claim that it holds without exception is not.
catalog_quote: §3. Удареніе въ чанскомъ ставится обыкновенно на второмъ слогѣ съ конца ... Отступленіе отъ этой нормы наблюдается въ слѣдующихъ случаяхъ: а) сложные глаголы удареніе ставятъ на огласовку предлога, которая часто бываетъ не во второмъ, а третьемъ съ конца слогѣ, и тогда удареніе переносится на этотъ третій съ конца слогъ ... 1) отрицательная частица ... воспринимаясь проклитически, какъ приставка …
readall_conflicts: No two opened sources disagree, because the only listed work (Lacroix 2018) could not be opened and the item its open_url actually resolves to (Lacroix 2011, ditransitives) is silent on stress. The one substantive check available is Lacroix's 2009 Lyon 2 thesis on the Arhavi dialect, already held by the project from the compilers, not in the listed works). It agrees with the catalog's penultimate rule for nominals (nouns, adjectives, adverbs, demonstratives, non-finite verb forms), but it limits the uniform penult rule in scope: in finite verb forms stress is morphologically determined (negation, preverbs and the causative suffixes -ap/-in attract it; otherwise the root is stressed, with lexically fixed position inside polysyllabic roots), and can fall on any syllable except the last -- e.g. mó-xt-ase 'he will come', doló-b-il-i 'I entered' are not penult-stressed. Gordon's catalog row (penultimate stress) therefore describes the nominal rule and over-generalises for finite verbs; this is a scope refinement rather than a contradiction of the penult placement itself.

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (not in the strict set, in the dominant set), rule penult kept as the default: penultimate in nominals over the domain base-plural-case-additive (clitics/possessives outside; surface final stress only via post-lexical final-vowel deletion and unassimilated Turkish loans); finite verbs morphologically accented (NEG var-/mo- or ko- > preverb > causative -ap/-in > root, lexical within bisyllabic roots), any syllable but the last — per Lacroix 2009 §2.3 pp.33-42, consistent with Marr 1910 §3(a), (1) and with StressTyp2's own verb/noun split. If the catalog prefers, 'morphological' is the alternative; 'fixed-strict' is not defensible.

sources.quote: "§3. Stress in Chan [Laz] is ordinarily placed on the second syllable from the end ... Deviation from this norm is observed in the following cases: (a) compound verbs place stress on the preverb vowel, which is often not in the second but the third syllable from the end, and then the stress moves to that third-from-the-end syllable." And: in Turkish loans the final syllable, stressed in Turkish, becomes penultimate and stressed in Chan.

sources.quote: Two word classes must be distinguished. Nominals (nouns, adjectives, adverbs, demonstratives, non-finite verb forms) of Laz origin: 'l'accent tombe sur la syllabe pénultième', domain = base-plural-case-additive particle; possessives and clitics -na/-ya outside the domain (bée-çkuni); final-vowel deletion applies after accent placement giving surface final stress (dalép, mzuğáş); unassimilated Turkish loans keep source stress (odá, deré-s). Finite verbs: 'l'accent peut frapper n'importe quelle syllabe sauf la dernière. C'est la structure morphologique du verbe qui détermine la place de l'accent

tone.quote: Le laze a un accent de mot distinctif, c'est-à-dire dont la position dans le mot contribue à identifier celui-ci. La prosodie du français, avec son accent final automatique, n'est pas une source de difficulté particulière.
tone.translation: Laz has a distinctive word accent, i.e. one whose position in the word helps identify the word. French prosody, with its automatic final accent, is not a particular source of difficulty.

tone.quote: In the case of Laz a wh-word is stressed, including the Muhajir Laz speech, the sentence is characterized by falling intonation contour. In a Georgian’s Laz speech from Borchkha, who has moved to Khopa after marriage as well as in the Laz speech of Hither Sarpi, a subject is stressed (აჲა aja). In Atinan, Artashenian and Vijan a verb is stressed and a sentence has rising intonation at the end.
